segments.narration: The reason you haven't opened a Roth IRA is probably wrong.

segments.heading: The fix
segments.narration: Make a payment a few days before the statement closes, so a smaller balance gets reported. Then pay the rest by the due date.

Fix: pay down before the statement closing date, then pay the rest by the due date. Utilization is based on recent balances, so it recovers quickly. Paying on time matters most.

script.title: How to start investing with $100 a month (beginner walkthrough)
script.hook: A hundred dollars a month doesn't sound like investing. Over forty years, it can quietly become one of the biggest things you own.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: A hundred dollars a month doesn't sound like investing. It sounds like a phone bill. But money invested in your twenties gets the one thing nobody can buy later: time. In this video we'll go from zero to an automated investing setup, in the order that actually makes sense. What to do before you invest, which account to open, what to buy inside it, how to automate it, and what to do the first time the market drops and your balance turns red. No individual company bets, no predictions, and no promises about returns. Just the setup that most people wish someone had shown them at twenty-two.
segments.on_screen_text: Investing $100 a month, start to finish
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes standing at the start of a long, gently winding garden path at sunrise. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why time matters
segments.narration: Here's a hypothetical to show the shape of it. Invest $100 a month for forty years, and assume an average of seven percent a year. You'd put in $48,000, and the account would be worth roughly $262,000. Start ten years later, same $100, same assumption, and you'd put in $36,000 and end up around $122,000. Ten fewer years cost more than half the result, because the growth in the final decades is growth on growth. Real markets don't deliver a smooth seven percent, and returns aren't promised. But the lesson holds: starting small and early usually beats starting big and late.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two coin trees, one planted earlier and much taller than the other, same-size watering cans. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: $100 a month at a hypothetical 7%
chart.note: Hypothetical 7% a year, compounded monthly; not a forecast

segments.heading: Before you invest
segments.narration: Two things come first. One: a starter emergency fund, even just $1,000 in a separate savings account, so a car repair doesn't land on a credit card. Two: deal with high-interest debt. If a credit card charges twenty-plus percent, paying it down is a known return of that rate, which is very hard to beat with investing. Lower-rate debt, like many federal student loans, is different; plenty of people invest while paying those on schedule. The order isn't moral. It's math: protect against surprises, kill the expensive debt, then grow.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three stepping stones: a small jar, a broken chain, then a sprouting plant. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step one: the match
segments.narration: If your employer offers a 401(k) match, that's usually the first place your money goes. A common formula is a fifty percent match on contributions up to six percent of pay. On a $45,000 salary, contributing six percent is $2,700 a year, and the employer adds $1,350. That's an immediate fifty percent on that money before any market movement. Log into your benefits portal, find the match formula, and set your contribution to at least that level. Also check the vesting schedule, which says how long you need to stay before the employer's money is fully yours. Your own contributions are always yours.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two jars pouring into one larger jar, a small gift bow on the second stream. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step two: the Roth IRA
segments.narration: No match, or already getting it? A Roth IRA is a strong next step for many people early in their careers. You contribute money you've already paid tax on, it grows, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. The 2026 limit is $7,500 if you're under fifty, so $100 a month, or $1,200 a year, fits easily. You need earned income, and there are income limits, so check the IRS page for the current numbers. You open a Roth IRA at a brokerage, not at your job, and it takes about fifteen minutes online.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes opening a small door in a garden wall with a sun icon above it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What to buy
segments.narration: This is where people freeze, so keep it boring. Two simple options. A target-date index fund with a year near when you'd turn sixty-five: one fund that holds stocks and bonds and gets more conservative over time. Or a broad total-market or S&P 500 index fund, which spreads your money across hundreds or thousands of companies. Either way, look up the expense ratio. Broad index funds from large providers often charge a few hundredths of a percent a year. If a fund charges one percent or more for the same kind of index exposure, keep looking. One or two funds is plenty. You don't need a collection.
segments.on_screen_text: Keep it boring: one or two index funds
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a single basket holding a mosaic of tiny squares, beside a small price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Automate it
segments.narration: Now remove yourself from the process. Set an automatic transfer of $100 from checking to your IRA the day after payday. Then, if your brokerage offers it, set automatic investing into your chosen fund, so the cash doesn't just sit there. That last part matters: depositing money and buying a fund are two different steps, and plenty of people discover months later that their money was parked in cash. After the first month, open the account and confirm you see shares of the fund, not just a cash balance. Then stop checking every day. Once a month is plenty.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a gentle conveyor belt carrying coins from a wallet into a basket. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your first downturn
segments.narration: At some point your balance will drop, maybe a lot. Broad stock markets have fallen twenty percent or more several times in recent decades, and they will again. When that happens, your automatic $100 is buying shares at lower prices, which is the plan working, not failing. The common mistake is selling after a drop, locking in the loss, and buying back after prices recover. Decide now, while things are calm, that you'll leave long-term money alone. If a balance drop would truly wreck you, that money probably belonged in savings, not stocks.

segments.heading: Growing past $100
segments.narration: A hundred dollars is a starting line, not a ceiling. The easiest way to grow it is to tie increases to events. Every raise, bump your contribution by half the raise. Every January, add one percent to your 401(k). When a debt is paid off, redirect that payment into investing. Many 401(k) plans offer an automatic yearly increase you can switch on in about a minute. You barely feel each step, but over a few years $100 a month can turn into $300 or $500 without a dramatic budget overhaul.

segments.heading: Mistakes to skip
segments.narration: A few traps catch beginners. Chasing whatever went up most last year; past performance doesn't predict next year. Owning eight funds that hold the same companies. Checking the app daily and reacting to noise. Pulling money out of a Roth IRA for non-emergencies, which costs you years of growth even when it's allowed. And leaving deposits uninvested in cash. None of these need special knowledge to avoid. They need a simple plan you set up once and a little patience.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Here's the whole thing on one screen. Build a starter emergency fund. Pay down high-interest debt. Get your full 401(k) match. Open a Roth IRA if you're eligible. Pick one or two low-cost index funds. Automate both the transfer and the purchase. Leave it alone when markets drop. Increase it whenever your income goes up. That's it. Not exciting, and that's the point. Everything here is education, not personal advice, so check the details against your own situation and the official sources in the description.

script.title: Feel behind on money? A 30-day reset plan
script.hook: Feeling behind with money is common. The fix isn't a dramatic overhaul. It's thirty days of small, specific moves.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you feel behind on money, you're in big company. Maybe friends seem to have savings, investments, a plan, and you've got a vague sense of dread every time you open your banking app. Here's the thing: 'behind' usually isn't a number problem first. It's a visibility problem. You can't fix what you avoid looking at. So this is a thirty-day reset. Each week has a focus, and each day's task takes under thirty minutes. By day thirty, you'll know your numbers, have a spending system, a debt plan, a starter emergency fund under way, and a retirement account switched on.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes standing at the bottom of a short, friendly staircase with four landings. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Days 1–3: see it all
segments.narration: Day one: list every account. Checking, savings, every credit card, student loans, car loan, buy-now-pay-later plans, retirement accounts from old jobs. Day two: write the balance and interest rate next to each one. Day three: subtract what you owe from what you have. That number is your net worth, and in your twenties it's often negative, especially with student loans. Take Jordan, a fictional example. Checking and savings add up to $1,800, and an old retirement account holds $2,500. Jordan owes $3,200 on a card and $14,000 in student loans. That's $4,300 minus $17,200: a net worth of minus $12,900. That's okay. It's a starting point, not a grade. The goal of these three days is only this: no more mystery. Most people find the real number is less scary than the fog they'd been carrying around.

segments.heading: Days 4–7: watch, don't change
segments.narration: For the next four days, just track spending. Every purchase, written down or screenshotted, no changes yet. You're collecting real data instead of guessing. On day seven, also pull your free credit reports from AnnualCreditReport.com, the official site, and skim them for accounts you don't recognize or late payments that look wrong. Your report is the raw material for your credit score, and errors do happen. Reading it takes twenty minutes and costs nothing. End the week with a short note: what surprised you most?

segments.heading: Week 2: shrink fixed costs
segments.narration: Week two is about fixed costs, because cutting one recurring bill pays off every month without any willpower. Day eight: do a subscription audit. Search ninety days of statements for recurring charges and cancel anything you forgot existed. Day nine: call or chat with your phone carrier and car insurer and ask what lower plans or discounts exist. Quotes from two competitors give you leverage. Day ten: set up two checking accounts, one for bills that's auto-funded on payday, and one for everything else. Fixed costs handled once can stay handled.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a pair of scissors trimming a long chain of small recurring loops. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Week 2: one weekly number
segments.narration: Day eleven: take your take-home pay, subtract fixed bills, subtract what you want to save, and what's left is flexible spending. Multiply that monthly amount by twelve and divide by fifty-two. That's your weekly spending number. Day twelve: move that amount to your spending account every Monday. Day thirteen and fourteen: live on it and notice what happens. Most people overspend in a predictable place, like delivery or weekend plans. You don't have to be perfect. You just need one number that tells you, mid-week, whether you're fine.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes refilling a small wallet on a Monday morning. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Week 3: a debt plan
segments.narration: Day fifteen: put all debts in a list from highest interest rate to lowest. Day sixteen: turn on autopay for at least the minimum on every single one, so you never miss a payment, since payment history is the biggest factor in most credit scores. Day seventeen: choose a method for extra money. Avalanche, highest rate first, saves the most interest. Snowball, smallest balance first, gets faster wins. Either beats paying minimums only. For federal student loans, use the Loan Simulator on studentaid.gov to see repayment plans that fit your income, because the options have changed recently.

segments.heading: Week 3: start the cushion
segments.narration: Days eighteen to twenty-one: open a separate savings account for emergencies at an insured bank or credit union. High-yield savings accounts often pay far more interest than a standard account at a big bank; check that it's FDIC or NCUA insured and has no monthly fee. Then set an automatic transfer, even $25 a week. The first goal is $1,000. The long-term goal is three to six months of essential expenses. This fund is what stops the next surprise from becoming new credit card debt, which is how a lot of people stay stuck.

segments.heading: Week 4: switch on retirement
segments.narration: Day twenty-two: log into your benefits portal. If there's a 401(k) match, set your contribution to at least the amount that gets the full match. Day twenty-three: track down old 401(k)s from previous jobs and make sure you know where they are. Days twenty-four and twenty-five: if you have no workplace plan, or already get the match, look at opening a Roth IRA, and choose a low-cost target-date or broad index fund inside it. Even $50 a month counts. You're not trying to catch up in one month. You're making sure time starts working on your side.

segments.heading: Week 4: protect what you built
segments.narration: Days twenty-six and twenty-seven: freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It's free, doesn't affect your score, and you can lift it temporarily when you apply for something. Day twenty-eight: set up three alerts in your bank and card apps: low balance, large transaction, and payment due five days ahead. Day twenty-nine: write down where every account lives and store passwords in a password manager. Protection isn't exciting, but one stolen identity or missed payment can undo months of progress.

segments.heading: Day 30: your first money date
segments.narration: Day thirty: do your first monthly money date. Twenty minutes. Open every account, compare this month's spending to your weekly number, adjust next month, and choose one new move. Then rerun your net worth from day three. It might have barely moved, and that's fine. What changed is that you now have systems: bills that pay themselves, a number to spend, a debt plan on autopay, a cushion that's growing and retirement money that's invested. Feeling behind fades when you can see the system working.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Here's the thirty days in one breath. Week one: list every account and track spending without judging. Week two: cut recurring costs, split your accounts and set a weekly spending number. Week three: autopay every minimum, pick a payoff method and start a separate emergency fund. Week four: get your 401(k) match, consider a Roth IRA, freeze your credit and turn on alerts. Then a twenty-minute money date every month. Comparing yourself to other people's highlight reels won't move your numbers. These steps will. And if you slip for a week, you don't restart from zero; you just pick up at the next day on the list.
